title: The top 15 party schools in the US, ranked
snippet:
Syracuse University was ranked as the seventh-best party school in the US.
Brett Carlsen/Getty Images

Niche ranked the best party colleges in the US based on student data about campus party culture.
A school's party scene can be a big draw for some incoming students.
Florida State University was ranked as the top party school for 2027.

From which schools offer the best classes to what kind of professional network they want to build, college decisions can be a complicated question for students and their families to navigate.
But for some students, it also comes down to one thing: where they'll have the most fun outside class.
This year, Florida State University is the place to be. It was ranked the No. 1 party school in the US for 2027 by Niche.
Some schools hold large events during homecoming or football seasons, while others keep them going year-round. One school, the University of Miami, for example, has a boat-burning ceremony in which scores of students gather around Lake Osceola in Coral Gables, Florida, to watch a boat burn as part of homecoming events.
At some schools, party culture centers on tailgating and football games, while at others, large off-campus parties are the main social events.
Every year, Niche publishes a list of the best party schools in the US as part of its annual best colleges list. The site uses student surveys of the party scene on campus, ratings for athletics and Greek life, and access to bars and restaurants based on US Census data to determine the ranking.
Whether it's large state schools or smaller colleges with tight-knit communities, these are the 15 schools across the US where students party the hardest in 2026 and 2027.

15. Howard University in Washington, DC

The Washington Post/The Washington Post via Getty Images


Howard University, a historically Black college, was named the 15th-best party school in the US.
Known as "The Mecca," the school is the alma mater of key figures such as Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall, but that doesn't mean that students sacrifice fun for academics.
The Washington, DC, school has a large and engaged Greek life scene. Some students attend "Thirsty Thursdays" parties or darties (day parties) between classes, The Root reported.
"The good parties are off campus," one student wrote on Niche. "If you're not a party person, there are so many organizations to be a part of, so you will find your people."


14. Syracuse University in Syracuse, New York

Nate Shron/Getty Images


Syracuse University was ranked the 14th-best party school in the nation by Niche.
Before the COVID-19 pandemic, students marked the end of the school year with Mayfest, a celebration that featured performances and parties. While the tradition hasn't returned, it has inspired different events at the end of the spring semester, such as 2023's "Block Darty."
Even as traditions change, Syracuse has kept its party-school reputation thanks to its large Greek life scene.
In October, students celebrate homecoming with tailgates, networking events, and open house tours of campus buildings.
"The party culture is very fun," one student wrote on Niche, while another added that "the overall culture was overly centered around Greek life and partying."


13. University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa, Alabama

Jackson Laizure/Getty Images


With 71 social Greek life chapters, the University of Alabama has been one of the nation's largest fraternity and sorority communities in terms of active membership since 2021.
"Bama Rush," a 2023 documentary, took viewers inside the high-stakes world of sororities at the school, showing the fashion, culture, and shortcomings of Greek-life recruitment.
"I have loved the first few weeks that I have been part of the UA community," a university freshman wrote on Niche, adding that they'd "made connections with students from all over the country, and that has been an eye-opening experience for me."


12. University of Texas—Austin in Austin
The University of Texas—Austin also ranked as a top party school.
David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images


At UT Austin, the party scene often centers on game days, campus traditions, and the bars and venues along nearby West Campus and Sixth Street.
Football weekends during the fall bring students, alumni, and visitors together for tailgates, concerts, and late-night celebrations across the city.
"The party scene is also just as lively as the people here. You'll always be able to find an event on weekends, from frat/sorority house parties to student organization events and an iconic bar street," one freshman wrote on Niche.


11. Morgan State University in Baltimore
The Morgan State University marching band is nationally renowned.
TIMOTHY A. CLARY / AFP via Getty Images


Morgan State University in Baltimore ranked 11th in Niche's national ranking.
Students at the HBCU often gather for large block parties and daytime events, while homecoming brings an even bigger campus-wide celebration. The annual festivities typically include major concerts, alumni events, and parties across campus.
"The party life is very lively, there's always something going on, and there is literally something at Morgan for EVERYBODY," one freshman wrote on Niche.


10. University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in Champaign, Illinois

Icon Sportswire/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images


Famous for its party-school reputation, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign ranked 10th among party schools.
The school, which is also ranked the best public university in Illinois by Niche, has repeatedly been ranked a top party school. In 2015, the then-university chancellor, Phyllis Wise, told CNN that the school wasn't proud of the label.
Still, students enjoy a vibrant party culture, which includes the famous Unofficial Saint Patrick's Day celebration during the first week of March, when students party through the weekend in an alternative to the traditional Saint Patrick's Day, which falls during the school's spring break.
One student on Niche described the school as the "definition of study hard, party harder," while another wrote that "the party scene is amazing," and the school is "overall a great place to go to college if you are willing to be outgoing."


9. West Virginia University in Morgantown, West Virginia

Greg Fiume/NCAA Photos via Getty Images


West Virginia University also made it to the top 10, after Niche named it the ninth-best party school in the US.
Located in Morgantown, the school's social life is shaped by Mountaineers athletics, Greek life, and campus traditions. Its Greek community hosts more than 70 social, professional, academic, service, interest-based, and honorary fraternal organizations, per the school.
"West Virginia University is a big school with a lot to offer for many different people," one student wrote on Niche. "I would recommend it to someone who is willing to go out of their way to find their community. Due to the size and party nature of the school, it can be easy to feel isolated if you don't fit in with the average WVU student. Otherwise, the nature and campus are beautiful, and the academics are great."
Another student on the site highlighted the school's other "types of fun ways to spend the night that don't have to involve alcohol" like the free, late-night UpAllNight event hosted by the school every weekend over the fall and spring semesters, which puts on free events like game shows, bingo, trivia, bowling, billiards, and other activities for students who want to party without the alcohol.


8. University of Georgia in Athens, Georgia

Icon Sportswire/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images


The University of Georgia in Athens, Georgia, was ranked the eighth-best party school in the nation.
The school's party reputation comes partly from its large Greek life scene, in which over 30% of undergrad students participate, the Red and Black student newspaper reported. The school also has a large football fan base, and every year, students and alums celebrate homecoming with parades, tailgates, and other events.
"Although the academics are hard, the party scene and friendships made will be worth it all," one student wrote on Niche.


7. The Ohio State University in Columbus, Ohio
Ohio State ranked 20th on Niche's ranking.
Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images


The social scene on campus at Ohio State is vibrant, with Buckeyes football, student organizations, and Greek life often filling up students' free time.
The school's homecoming celebrations are large and historic, with the tradition dating back to 1912. Celebrations last a week and include alumni reunions and a parade.
"It is a great school if you are looking to party, be involved, and get a good education," one student wrote on Niche.


6. The Pennsylvania State University in University Park, Pennsylvania

Brett Carlsen/Getty Images


Penn State was ranked the sixth-best party school in the US.
Student life at the University Park school is often defined by football, Greek life, and student-led traditions like THON, a student-run charity dance marathon in which 400 student organizations and over 16,000 students participate each year, per the school.
"There's always something happening, whether it's a club event, a speaker, a game, or just a random Tuesday that turns into a great night with friends," one student wrote on Niche.


5. University of Southern California in Los Angeles

Icon Sportswire/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images


The University of Southern California in Los Angeles was ranked the fifth-best party school in the US.
The school, which has an acceptance rate of only 10% and a total cost of attendance of over $100,000, per its website, has one of the largest college football teams in the western US.
Each year, students welcome the Trojans back to Los Angeles during a weeklong homecoming celebration.
Part of the school's party ranking is thanks to its large Greek life scene, which often hosts parties at fraternity houses, welcoming students and their parents, including Will Ferrell.
"The social and party life is unmatched," one student wrote on Niche.


4. University of Dayton in Dayton, Ohio

Michael Hickey/Getty Images


The Catholic school balances religious life with its party scene and has a student experience shaped by Greek life, 240 student organizations, athletics, and on-campus student housing, which some students opt for during all four years of undergrad.
One of the largest events at the school is Christmas on Campus, when the campus community gathers to welcome children from the Dayton community to a tree-lighting ceremony, a mass, winter displays, and seasonal foods like hot cocoa and decorated cookies.
"You won't feel as if you don't have a friend," one student wrote on Niche.
"Partying and the weekend are a big part of campus life," another said. One student mentioned that the weekend often starts as early as Wednesday for students at the school.


3. University of Wisconsin—Madison in Madison, Wisconsin
The University of Wisconsin Madison students at a 2021 football game between Notre Dame Fighting Irish and the Wisconsin Badgers at Solider Field in Chicago.
Icon Sportswire/Dan Sanger/Getty Images


The University of Wisconsin—Madison was ranked third on the list.
Students at UW—Madison have access to various social activities, including recreational, leadership-based, and philanthropic activities. The school also has more than 60 Greek organizations.
"There is a good campus life and downtown Madison is a great place for socializing and interacting with others," one college junior wrote about the school on Niche. "Most people here want to see you succeed, and it is a very enjoyable experience."


2. Tulane University in New Orleans

Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images


Tulane University, which The Wall Street Journal ranked the top party school last year, is the second-best party school on Niche's 2027 list and the sixth-best school for Greek life in the US, per Niche's 2027 ranking.
Famous for its spirited campus atmosphere, especially during Mardi Gras, this New Orleans university enjoys its party-school reputation because of its location and front-row access to the city's vibrant culture.
In addition to off-site bars and eateries, the college has 25 Greek chapters and more than 200 social clubs, such as the Just Dance Club, the Improv Club, and even a crochet club.
One college freshman summarized it best: "The school is the definition of work hard, play hard(er)!"


1. Florida State University in Tallahassee, Florida

Butch Dill/Getty Images


The best party school is Florida State, which also ranked as the best school for Greek life in the US in another Niche ranking.
Sports are a huge part of campus life, with many students supporting a variety of athletics, from football to golf. When they're not rooting for their fellow classmates, students at FSU enjoy being part of the more than 700 clubs on campus.
"FSU is a place that accommodates many lifestyles and types of people," a college sophomore wrote on Niche, emphasizing that students with wide-ranging interests could enjoy themselves. "You can have an amazing time here without taking a sip of alcohol or ever going to any of the many nightclubs because there's always something happening right on campus."

title: Wall Street already loves ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is doubling down.
snippet:
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

OpenAI announced a ChatGPT product specifically for financial services on Thursday.
The product aims to surface better financial data for bankers and analysts.
Many banks and financial institutions, like Morgan Stanley, adopted ChatGPT early on.

ChatGPT's role on Wall Street is evolving.
OpenAI announced ChatGPT for Financial Services on Thursday, its latest foray into crafting AI tools for specific sectors. The product will bring a new glut of financial data directly into ChatGPT and provide bankers with a new way to check the tool's work.
As OpenAI prepares for a gigantic initial public offering expected in 2027, its latest release fits into two of its larger strategies: selling tools companies can use to automate work and building on its core AI products with industry-specific offerings.
The finance industry has already started embracing AI tools. Morgan Stanley adopted ChatGPT early on, and leaders across Wall Street are pouring time and money into figuring out new ways to use AI.
OpenAI's new product will let users work with financial datasets from Daloopa, PitchBook, and LSEG News without needing separate contracts or subscriptions. The company says bringing this data under the hood of ChatGPT will get analysts information more quickly and in better formats.
Financial analysts will also get a new way to check ChatGPT's data work. They can get "granular citations" for information, letting them "trace figures and claims back to their sources, and check the evidence as their analysis develops," OpenAI's press release said.
OpenAI said it has improved its existing financial data features in ChatGPT and is working to add data from other providers, such as S&P Capital IQ, Factiva, and Moody's.
GPT-6 Astra, the company's latest model, can retrieve the right information, run financial analyses, and then synthesize those findings, OpenAI wrote.
The company plans to use this launch and its partnerships with banks to make more improvements down the road, saying it will train its models to "find, interpret, and use this data like we know the best analysts can."
Sarah Friar, the chief financial officer steering OpenAI through the buildup to its IPO, teased the financial services announcement at a Goldman Sachs conference on Tuesday. She named the banking focus alongside areas like chip design, life sciences, personal finance, and health.

title: My family of 5 just moved out of my parents' house. We miss seeing them every day, and they're experiencing empty nest 2.0.
snippet:
The author and her family lived with her parents for five months.
Courtesy of Melissa Noble

My family of five lived in my parents' house for five months before moving out. 
My dad was diagnosed with Parkinson's Disease, and we wanted them to have their space back.
It's been an adjustment living in our own home again.

The first thing I noticed was the silence. Waking up in our new home, we found it so quiet in the mornings.
Whereas a few weeks ago, I'd hear my dad shuffling around upstairs making his early-morning tea, or my mom listening to Reels, our house was suddenly deathly quiet before the kids opened their eyes.
August marked five months since we began living with my folks in my childhood home. They'd kindly offered my family of five the bottom level of their two-story house after we relocated from country Victoria in Australia to the Gold Coast, where I grew up.
The multi-generational living arrangement worked really well and was a success overall. But when my dad was diagnosed with Parkinson's Disease in June, we decided it was time for us to move on. In August, we moved into our own home, about 10 minutes' drive from my parents.
Since our multigenerational living experience has come to an end, the feelings that have bubbled to the surface have been interesting. Happiness, sadness, guilt, and relief all at once.
I know that we couldn't continue living with my parents forever. They're 77 and 81. They need their own space and vice versa. But the feeling is generally bittersweet.
The author, her husband, and her kids enjoyed living with her parents.
Courtesy of Melissa Noble

We've gained a lot since moving out
In our new home, we can all totter around in our undies, without having to worry about feeling awkward. If my husband and I have a blow-up, there's nobody within earshot, and I think that we are getting on better in general now that we have our own space.
Our three kids also have their own rooms, which they are really enjoying (they were all piled into one bedroom at my folks' place). We no longer have to worry about the children being disruptive or navigate challenges like illnesses, different routines, or keeping shared spaces clean and tidy all the time.
Having privacy again is a simple pleasure I really missed.
But there are also a few things we've lost
While I love solitude and am generally introverted, I find myself missing certain aspects of multi-generational living. My morning cups of tea with my dad, for example, when we'd sit on his veranda and chat in the sunshine, or not talk at all.
I also miss the lunchtime discussions with Mom. Even if it was for 15 minutes lying on her bed and having a laugh about something silly.
Though we try to drop in and visit Mom and Dad regularly, we don't necessarily see them every day. I'm hoping that in the long run, we'll have quality time together, rather than quantity.
They live in a new neighborhood now, 10 minutes from her parents.
Courtesy of Melissa Noble

My folks are having mixed feelings, too
I know without a doubt that my folks adore our kids, but I do think they were finding it a bit much toward the end of our living arrangement. They, too, are relieved, but sad it's over.
At one point, before we moved out, Mom mentioned she was looking forward to having her house back, then felt guilty about her comments and tried to backtrack. The very next day, she was begging us to stay an extra week.
I think for Mom, who struggled with empty-nest syndrome when my siblings and I moved out, this whole situation has been a bit like empty-nest 2.0. Their house has gone from being a hive of activity, with grandchildren doing cartwheels in the living room and having laughing fits after dinner, to eerily quiet.
It's an adjustment we're navigating together
Living with my parents again after so many years apart was a gift, even if there were challenges. I think what makes this next chapter bittersweet is that we didn't leave because we hated each other's company; we left because we love my folks enough not to want to be a burden on them.
While we no longer share a roof, I'm hoping we can continue making memories and really enjoy the time we do spend together. I'm making a concerted effort to invite my folks over for weekly dinners, and we may even start a monthly family games night.
My mom and dad were my first home, and they will always be welcome in ours.

title: The NFL is about to test the best way to survive a brutal work trip
snippet:
Martin KEEP / AFP via Getty Images

The 49ers and Rams took very different approaches to getting to their upcoming game in Melbourne.
The 49ers have been in Australia for a week. The Rams opted for a last-minute arrival.
The two strategies highlight the different ways people tackle work trips. 

Wondering about the best way to plan your next work trip? A bunch of football players might hold the answer.
The San Francisco 49ers take on the Los Angeles Rams Thursday in a clash of divisional rivals AND warring ideologies over the best way to travel for work.
The game kicks off from Melbourne, Australia, at 8:35 p.m. ET on Netflix because the NFL won't stop until it has more money than God growing its global football fandom. International games aren't new to the league, but the 17-hour time difference between Melbourne and California makes for a massive travel challenge.
And the teams playing are taking very different approaches to their roughly 16-hour flights.
The 49ers got to Melbourne almost a week ago, choosing to arrive early to acclimate to the time change. The Rams, meanwhile, departed LA on Tuesday night, arriving roughly 24 hours before kickoff. When it's all said and done, they'll spend about as much time traveling to and from Melbourne as they do actually being there.
It's a strategy both teams have used before.
In recent years, the 49ers have avoided traveling home four different times when they've had back-to-back games far from San Francisco. Last year, the Rams didn't get to London until about 30 hours before kickoff, choosing to set up camp in Baltimore, where they had played the previous week.
Both approaches were successful — the 49ers went 7-1 on those four road trips, and the Rams swept their games in Baltimore and London.
But Australia is a completely different animal.
No right answers when traveling for work
The Rams and 49ers' differing approaches highlight the wide range of opinions people have on the best way to travel.
At the World Economic Forum in Switzerland this year, I asked executives for tips for long-haul flights. There wasn't a consensus.
"Just sleep whenever you can," David Steinbach, Global Chief Investment Officer at Hines, told me in January. "It is a deficit, and you just try to build it back anyway you can."
"I don't try to get on any time. I just kind of let the body guide you," he added.
Meanwhile …
"My biggest thing is getting on the plane and immediately going into the time zone I'm going into," Lisa Stevens, Aon's Chief Administrative Officer, told me. "I don't oversleep."
(For what it's worth, I try getting sleep on red-eye flights right away. But I'll be damned if I won't accept a free meal when they start handing them out.)
One thing the two NFL teams did agree on: How to get there. The Rams and 49ers both took the Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger aircraft. In a video from inside the plane, Rams player Byron Young called the setup "boujee."
On the field … or conference hall
You might argue that either team's success or failure doesn't correlate with the work most of us do. I die a little inside when executives compare themselves to professional athletes in LinkedIn posts, but the physical and mental aspects of work travel weigh on us all.
You might not need to run a 40-yard dash, but you will get your steps in at a spread-out conference. And you're wrong if you don't think the NFL is a thinking man's game. Can you identify split-field zone coverage that's been disguised with some fake blitzes? Didn't think so.
Don't rush to book your work trip based on tonight's results, though. Jet lag can have a long tail, something the 49ers have seen firsthand. San Francisco went 1-3 in the next game after those four extended road trips I mentioned before.
Bill Simmons, a sports media personality who has talked about this topic extensively, said he could see the 49ers winning tonight but struggling in the weeks to come as they readjust after their long acclimation in Australia.
As for oddsmakers, they're giving the edge to the Rams, who are 3.5-point favorites. That means the Rams need to win by at least 4 points for your bet to hit. (I wouldn't take that action, but I'm also not in a position to be giving anyone gambling advice.)
It's tough to read too much into the odds since the Rams are viewed as the favorite to win the Super Bowl. 
But if they get that far, they won't have to worry about travel logistics.
This season's Super Bowl is being held at SoFi Stadium … home to the Los Angeles Rams.

title: Gas prices are climbing again. See the states where it is the most and least expensive.
snippet:
The average price of a gallon of regular gas spiked past $4, according to AAA.
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Drivers are getting an unwelcome September surprise at the pump.
Escalating Middle East tensions have kept oil prices elevated since March.
An analyst warns high gas prices have filtered into retail shocks — and could hurt small businesses.

Filling up is getting more painful by the day.
The national average price for a gallon of regular gas rose to $4.28 on Thursday, up 6 cents in 24 hours and 13 cents over the past two days, according to AAA.
That's $1.08 more per gallon than drivers were paying a year ago.



The price jump comes as the six-month war between the US and Iran enters another dangerous new phase for global oil supplies.
US forces have struck several Iranian oil tankers in recent days, while Iran has attacked ships and a US base in Jordan on Tuesday. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have also set Saudi oil facilities ablaze and threatened shipping in the Red Sea.
Those attacks have further squeezed a market already strained by the near-shutdown of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that carried roughly 20% of the world's oil before the war.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose above $100 a barrel on Wednesday and Thursday, though it remains below its April wartime high of $126.41. Before the escalating conflict, Brent prices had stayed below $100 a barrel since 2022.
Now, drivers are feeling it from coast to coast. California had the country's highest average regular-gas price on Thursday, at $5.89 a gallon, according to AAA. Indiana had the lowest, at $3.56.
Diesel, a key cost for trucking and freight, hit a record national average of $5.94 a gallon. That, economists warn, has added to inflation beyond the pump.



Carol Spieckerman, a retail analyst, told Business Insider that the impact of higher gas prices is "far-reaching and underestimated" for the entire US economy. She said that higher fuel costs have led to higher prices for airline tickets, groceries, and petroleum-based products — and those higher prices are harder for small businesses to weather.
"If you're a specialty retailer in a single market, higher gas prices mean fewer shopping trips and more cautious spending when customers do show up," she said.
"By comparison, retailers like Walmart that serve as convenient one-stop shops and offer delivery in many areas will benefit. Amazon, which requires no travel at all, obviously gains ground."
For now, Americans are once again confronting a familiar reality: higher costs everywhere — from the checkout line to the gas pump.
